body:
Meaning of Home Rule

The Home Rule Movement was an important phase of the Indian national movement that developed during the First World War. Its central demand was that Indians should have the right to govern their own country instead of remaining under the direct political control of British officials.

Home Rule

Home Rule meant self-government for India within the British Empire. Indians would exercise greater control over their legislative and administrative affairs through representative institutions. The movement sought this change through constitutional and political methods.

The idea was influenced by the Irish Home Rule movement, which demanded self-government for Ireland within the United Kingdom. Indian nationalists adapted the principle to their own circumstances.

Home Rule was not the same as complete independence. The Home Rule Leagues sought self-government while maintaining India's connection with the British Empire. The Indian National Congress formally adopted the goal of Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, much later, at its Lahore session in December 1929.

Political Background Before 1916

The Surat Split of 1907

The Indian National Congress had divided into Moderate and Extremist groups at its Surat session in 1907. Surat is located in present-day Gujarat.

The Moderates generally preferred petitions, resolutions, constitutional demands and persuasion. Leaders such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak advocated more assertive political methods, including boycott, Swadeshi and public mobilisation.

After the split, the Moderates dominated the Congress organisation, while Tilak and his supporters remained outside its main organisational structure. The division weakened coordinated nationalist activity.

Tilak's Return in 1914

Bal Gangadhar Tilak returned to active Indian politics after his release from imprisonment in Mandalay, Burma, in 1914. He sought to reunite the nationalist groups because a divided Congress could not effectively press the demand for self-government.

Annie Besant, a London-born British political activist who had settled in India and was associated with the Theosophical Society, also worked to revive nationalist activity and bring the Congress factions together.

At the Bombay Congress session of December 1915, organisational changes permitted the return of the Extremist nationalists. Their reunion became clearly visible at the Lucknow Congress session of 1916.

Impact of the First World War

The First World War began in 1914 and continued until 1918. Britain involved India in the war without consulting a representative Indian government.

India contributed soldiers, resources and money to the British war effort. Military expenditure increased, taxes and wartime financial demands placed pressure on the economy, and rising prices created hardship for ordinary people.

The war also created a political opportunity. Indian nationalists argued that a country contributing substantially to Britain's war effort should receive meaningful rights of self-government.

The Home Rule leaders therefore treated wartime conditions as an opportunity to intensify the demand for political reform rather than postpone it indefinitely.

Why a New Movement Was Needed

After the decline of the Swadeshi agitation and the divisions within Congress, nationalists needed organisations that could maintain continuous political activity between annual Congress sessions.

Tilak and Besant believed that people should be educated about their political rights through newspapers, public meetings, local committees and political discussions.

Their immediate objective was to turn the demand for self-government into an organised public campaign.

Prelims focus

  • 1907: The Moderate–Extremist split occurred at the Surat Congress session.
  • 1914: The First World War began, and Tilak returned from imprisonment.
  • 1915: The Bombay Congress session permitted the return of Extremist nationalists.
  • 1916: Tilak and Annie Besant established separate Home Rule Leagues.
  • Trap: Home Rule in 1916 meant self-government within the British Empire, not the complete independence formally demanded by Congress in 1929.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, 2020–21 edition, printed pp. 112–115; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World – II, Class 10, Chapter 3, Nationalism in India, printed p. 54; D. Subramanyam Reddy, Outlines of Indian History, Chapter 38, Home Rule Movement, INFLIBNET, accessed 21 November 2026; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, entries for 1915 and 1916, accessed 21 November 2026.]

title: Background: Why the Home Rule Movement Emerged

body:
Formation of the Home Rule Leagues

In 1916, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant established 2 separate Home Rule Leagues. Both organisations sought self-government for India, but they operated through different leadership structures and geographical areas.

The leagues were not simply 2 branches of a single organisation. They worked independently while supporting the same political objective.

Tilak's Indian Home Rule League

Tilak established his Home Rule League in April 1916 at the Bombay Provincial Conference held at Belgaum, in present-day Karnataka.

The league was organised from Poona, now Pune. Its principal sphere of activity included Maharashtra, excluding Bombay city, Karnataka, the Central Provinces and Berar.

Tilak travelled widely, addressing public meetings and explaining why Indians should govern themselves. His reputation as a nationalist leader helped the movement attract support.

Joseph Baptista served as the league's first President, while N. C. Kelkar served as Secretary.

Tilak also used political journalism to promote nationalist ideas. His important newspapers were Kesari, published in Marathi, and Mahratta, published in English.

Annie Besant's All India Home Rule League

Annie Besant established her Home Rule League in September 1916, with its headquarters at Adyar, Madras, now part of Chennai.

Her league operated across the remaining areas of India, including Bombay city. It developed numerous local branches and used existing networks of political workers and Theosophical associates to spread the demand for self-government.

Important associates included George Arundale, the Organising Secretary, B. P. Wadia and C. P. Ramaswamy Aiyar.

Besant promoted the movement through public speeches, pamphlets, meetings and her publications New India and Commonweal.

Comparison of the 2 Leagues

FeatureTilak's LeagueBesant's League
FounderBal Gangadhar TilakAnnie Besant
FormationApril 1916September 1916
Place associated with formationBelgaumMadras
HeadquartersPoonaAdyar, Madras
Main geographical sphereMaharashtra excluding Bombay city, Karnataka, Central Provinces and BerarRemaining areas, including Bombay city
Important newspapersKesari and MahrattaNew India and Commonweal
OrganisationRelatively compact and centrally organisedBroader network of local branches

Why Were There 2 Leagues?

Tilak and Besant had different groups of followers and established organisational networks. Rather than delaying the movement by trying to combine these networks, they agreed to work in complementary geographical spheres.

This arrangement enabled both leaders to campaign for Home Rule without regularly competing for the same organisational territory.

Both leagues advocated constitutional political activity. They relied primarily on education, speeches, public opinion and organised pressure rather than an armed uprising.

Identify the correct leader

Tilak: April 1916, Belgaum, Poona, Kesari and Mahratta.

Besant: September 1916, Madras, Adyar, New India and Commonweal.

Prelims focus

  • Tilak's Home Rule League was founded in April 1916 at Belgaum.
  • Annie Besant's Home Rule League was established in September 1916.
  • Tilak's organisational headquarters were at Poona.
  • Besant's headquarters were at Adyar, Madras.
  • George Arundale was an important organiser of Besant's league.
  • Trap: Bombay city belonged to Besant's principal organisational sphere, although Tilak's league worked in other parts of the Bombay Presidency.

[Sources: Maharashtra State Gazetteers, The Home Rule Movement, sections Home Rule League for Maharashtra and High Court Justifies Tilak's Activities, accessed 21 November 2026; D. Subramanyam Reddy, Outlines of Indian History, Chapter 38, Home Rule Movement, INFLIBNET, accessed 21 November 2026; Bipan Chandra and others, India's Struggle for Independence, Chapter 13, The Home Rule Movement and Its Fallout, online text consulted 21 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Tilak’s and Besant’s separate Home Rule leagues worked in complementary areas, educated and mobilised people, and pursued the same goal.
pictures.caption: Separate organisations, complementary activity and one political goal.

title: The Two Home Rule Leagues of 1916: Tilak and Annie Besant

body:
How the Home Rule Leagues Spread Nationalist Ideas

The Home Rule Leagues attempted to create sustained public support for self-government. Their work was based on the belief that political change required an informed and organised population.

Instead of limiting political activity to annual Congress sessions or formal resolutions, the leagues encouraged local participation throughout the year.

Political Education and Public Meetings

League workers organised meetings, lectures and discussions to explain the demand for Home Rule. They described how British administration operated and why greater Indian representation was necessary.

Public meetings also allowed people outside the established political leadership to hear nationalist arguments and become involved in local activities.

Newspapers and Pamphlets

Printed literature was a major instrument of mobilisation.

Newspapers carried political arguments to readers, while pamphlets explained particular demands in relatively accessible language. League workers distributed material in English and Indian languages.

Tilak's organisation published material in Marathi, English and other regional languages, including Gujarati and Kannada. Besant's supporters circulated extensive political literature through their network.

Local Branches and Reading Rooms

Local league branches held discussions, established reading facilities, distributed literature and recruited supporters.

These activities helped connect political organisations in major cities with smaller towns and some rural areas.

Students, teachers, lawyers, journalists and other educated people were important participants. The movement also attempted to extend political awareness beyond these groups, but its social reach remained more limited than the larger mass movements that developed after 1919.

The Gujarat Connection

Gujarat's connection with the Home Rule period was not confined to the earlier Surat Congress split of 1907. Political workers associated with Gujarat also participated in the Home Rule propaganda networks.

Indulal Yagnik and the Young India Campaign

Indulal Yagnik, who later became a prominent public leader in Gujarat, was associated with the political publicity work surrounding the Home Rule campaign.

He worked with Jamnadas Dwarkadas and Shankerlal Banker in the group that established the Bombay publication Young India and supported the circulation of political pamphlets.

This early Home Rule-era publication should be distinguished from the later period when Mahatma Gandhi became associated with Young India.

The Home Rule League in Surat

A branch associated with Annie Besant's Home Rule network was established in Surat in September 1916, with assistance from local physician K. V. Vora.

The Surat branch initially attracted only a small group of supporters. Over time, local political leaders became more active, and public meetings helped popularise the demand for self-government.

Surat therefore provides a useful example of how a national political campaign reached an important city in Gujarat through local associations and organisers.

The distinction between the earlier Surat Congress split of 1907 and the Surat Home Rule activity beginning in 1916 is important. They were different developments in the history of the national movement.

Political Importance of the Mobilisation

The Home Rule campaign helped make self-government a subject of discussion beyond the highest levels of the Congress leadership.

Its public meetings, propaganda literature and local branches strengthened connections between nationalist workers and people interested in political reform.

The Home Rule Movement increased political participation, but it should not be described as having already achieved the scale of the later Non-Cooperation Movement. Its main strength lay in continuous political education, local organisation and the popularisation of self-government.

Prelims focus

  • Home Rule mobilisation relied on meetings, lectures, newspapers, pamphlets and local branches.
  • Indulal Yagnik was associated with the Bombay-based Young India publicity group.
  • Jamnadas Dwarkadas and Shankerlal Banker were associated with the same publicity effort.
  • A Home Rule branch was established in Surat in September 1916, with help from K. V. Vora.
  • Trap: The Home Rule Leagues were political mobilisation organisations; they were not legislative councils established by the British government.

[Sources: Bipan Chandra and others, India's Struggle for Independence, Chapter 13, The Home Rule Movement and Its Fallout, sections on league organisation and propaganda, online text consulted 21 November 2026; D. Subramanyam Reddy, Outlines of Indian History, Chapter 38, Home Rule Movement, INFLIBNET, accessed 21 November 2026; Douglas E. Haynes, Rhetoric and Ritual in Colonial India: The Shaping of a Public Culture in Surat City, 1852–1928, University of California Press, 1991, Chapter 9, World War I and the Crisis in Urban Authority, online text consulted 21 November 2026.]
